t: What is the patent status?
opts: Prior art search and patentability assessment completed
h: Why it matters: A patent still under application has uncertainty about grant; a granted patent provides full protection. EPO timeline: from application to grant typically takes 3–5 years. Tip: if still at application stage, consider the score in future terms once the patent is granted.

t: What is the legal strength of the patent?
opts: No prior art search carried out
Prior art search at a national patent office
Complete prior art and infringement search
h: What it measures: how defensible the patent is in case of challenge. A professional complete search (prior art + infringement) costs €3,000–€8,000 but significantly increases the patent's legal value. PCT: the international PCT search is the standard for multi-country patents.

t: How long is the patent still valid?
opts: More than 12 years of remaining life
h: Maximum term: 20 years from the filing date (Article 63 EPC). Pharmaceutical exception: a Supplementary Protection Certificate (SPC) can extend protection by up to 5 extra years. EPO annual fees: grow from ~€500 (year 3) to ~€1,800+ (year 10+); consider whether renewal is economically sustainable.

t: How broad and inclusive are the patent claims?
opts: Claims cover a general principle (core / platform technology)
h: What claims are: they define the legal monopoly space. The broader they are, the harder it is for competitors to work around them. Trade-off: overly broad claims may be invalidated for lack of support in the description. Recommended strategy: structure with a broad independent claim plus dependent fall-back claims.

t: Does the patent's geographical coverage include the relevant markets?
opts: Protection in a single national market
Protection in a few countries of the target market
Protection in all current market countries
Protection in all current and potentially relevant countries
h: Indicative costs: European patent (EPC) validated in 5 countries ≈ €15,000–€25,000 total over 10 years; global PCT considerably more. Priority countries for SMEs: DE, FR, GB, US, CN are often the most critical markets. Tip: cover at least the countries of key customers and the most dangerous competitors.

t: Is the patent monitored to identify potential infringements?
opts: Partial systematic monitoring of selected competing products
Formalised global monitoring with a dedicated watchdog
h: Available tools: automatic alerts on Espacenet / USPTO, patent watch services (€500–€3,000/year). Why it matters: without monitoring, infringements go undetected and the patent loses practical value. For SMEs: even an annual manual check of key competitors' products is better than no monitoring at all.

t: Are legal disputes frequent in the operating markets?
opts: Legal proceedings very frequent in the sector
Legal proceedings present in the sector
Legal disputes and proceedings not usual in the sector
h: Counter-intuitive note: a litigious sector lowers the score because defending the patent is costly and risky. High-litigation sectors: pharmaceuticals, ICT/software, semiconductors. Low-litigation sectors: many traditional manufacturing sectors. Litigation costs: patent proceedings in Europe can cost €50,000–€500,000+.

t: Does the company have the means to enforce patent rights?
opts: Generally too expensive and difficult to enforce rights
Rights defended only in selected countries in key markets
Rights defended in almost all cases unless too costly
h: Alternatives to litigation: patent mediation (WIPO) or arbitration clauses in contracts can reduce costs significantly. Patent insurance: products covering part of legal costs — premiums from €2,000–€10,000/year. For small companies: consider partnerships with specialist law firms on a success-fee basis.

t: Is the invention a unique technology in its field?
opts: The invention has a marginal effect compared to existing technology
The invention has some improvement over existing technology
The invention has a significant improvement over existing technology
The invention has a substantial improvement and is clearly innovative
The invention could change the way the sector operates
h: How to assess: compare with the state of the art at the time of filing. Signs of high uniqueness: no similar prior art, scientific publications citing the invention, interest from large companies in purchasing or licensing. Tip: request an FTO (Freedom to Operate) analysis to identify potentially blocking patents (cost €3,000–€8,000).

t: Is the invention technically superior to substitute technologies?
opts: The technology operates in a field dominated by new and more advanced substitute technologies
There is a wide range of fairly competitive substitute technologies
Substitute technologies exist but are limited in use and application
Substitute technologies exist but are not yet competitive
h: What substitute technologies are: different solutions that solve the same problem (e.g. streaming vs. DVD). Example: a patented packaging machine faces the "threat" of manual solutions or entirely different processes. Recommended analysis: map alternative technologies in the market and assess their maturity.

t: To what extent has the invention been tested?
opts: The invention has only been tested in theory (calculations/simulations)
Isolated experiments or tests have been carried out
h: Why it matters: the degree of technological maturity (TRL — Technology Readiness Level) directly influences commercial risk. Corresponding TRL: 1=TRL 1–3, 2=TRL 4, 3=TRL 5–6, 4=TRL 7–8, 5=TRL 9. For funders: Horizon Europe / EIC often evaluate TRL as a minimum eligibility requirement.

t: Does the patented technology require new skills or production equipment?
opts: Requires a completely new production process from scratch
Substantial development of production processes needed before it can be used
Some development of production processes needed
Only minor adaptations to existing processes needed
Can be used with current production technology without modifications
h: Impact on costs: a completely new process may require €100K–€2M+ in investment. Available support: Industry 4.0 initiatives, EIC / Horizon Europe grants, national R&D tax credit schemes. Tip: consider contract manufacturing (outsourced production) to reduce initial investment.

t: How much time is needed before the technology can be commercialised?
h: This value is used in the NPV calculation: it shifts the revenue horizon forward and reduces the net present value. Typical time components: product development, certifications (CE mark, ISO), regulatory approvals (EMA for medicines), production scaling. Tip: reducing time-to-market is often the best investment to maximise NPV.

t: Are counterfeit products easy to produce by competitors?
opts: The technology is easily identifiable, easy to copy and reproduce
The technology is easy to copy and produce
The technology is comparatively easy to identify, copy and produce
The technology is complex and difficult to copy and produce
The technology is complex and extremely difficult to copy and produce
h: Additional protection strategies: trade secret complementary to the patent, inherent technical complexity, exclusive supply chain. Positive example: technologies requiring special materials, high-precision processes or tacit know-how that is difficult to replicate. Legal note: trade secrets and know-how are protected under the EU Trade Secrets Directive (2016/943).

t: Are counterfeit products easy to identify?
opts: It is extremely difficult to identify counterfeit products
It is difficult but not impossible to identify counterfeit products
It is fairly easy to identify counterfeit products
It is easy to identify counterfeit products
It is extremely easy to identify counterfeit products
h: Why it matters: if infringement is easily detectable, competitors are more deterred and the patent has greater practical value. Detection tools: chemical/spectroscopic analysis, reverse engineering, visual/functional comparison, trade fair and catalogue monitoring. Sectors with low detectability: intermediate chemical processes, software, business methods.

t: Does deployment of the technology depend on licence agreements with third parties?
opts: Use of the patent depends on extensive licence agreements with competitors
Use depends on some licences with competitors
Use does not depend on particular licences with competitors
Licences needed but not with direct competitors
Use of the patent is completely independent of licence agreements
h: Patent thicket: in sectors such as ICT and pharmaceuticals, a technology commonly requires licences from dozens of third-party patents. FRAND: standard-essential patents (SEPs) must be licensed on Fair, Reasonable and Non-Discriminatory terms. Tip: verify via an FTO analysis whether in-licensing is needed before investing in product development.

t: Does the technology have marketing value towards customers (customer value)?
opts: The patent provides a product utility improvement very difficult to communicate to customers
The patent provides a communicable improvement in product utility
The patent provides distinctive features that can be actively used in marketing
h: Trade mark vs. patent: the patent protects the technology, but its marketing value materialises when it becomes a differentiator perceived by the customer. Examples of high communicability: "patented engine 30% more efficient", "patented material 2x stronger". Strategic integration: combine the patent with registered design and trade mark for comprehensive IP protection.

t: What are the commercialisation options for the technology?
opts: No known market exists for the patented technology
The technology has not yet been targeted at a specific market
A consolidated market exists for the technology
A consolidated market exists with further well-defined market options
A consolidated market exists with other emerging and tangible markets
h: Commercialisation channels: direct sale, licensing, technology franchising, joint venture, spin-off. Market sizing: assess TAM (total addressable market), SAM (serviceable), SOM (realistic target). Available support: EEN (Enterprise Europe Network) and EIC for finding international commercial partners.

t: What is the market growth in the business area where the technology is used?
h: This value enters the NPV calculation as the turnover growth rate of the business area. Benchmark 2024: traditional manufacturing 1–3%, medical/pharma 5–8%, cleantech/renewables 8–15%, AI/digital 10–20%. Suggested sources: Eurostat, sector federation reports, IBISWorld / Statista market reports.

t: What is the expected market life of the technology after commercialisation?
h: This value enters the NPV calculation as the horizon for additional cash flows. Factors reducing market life: rapid technological obsolescence, strong competition, regulatory changes. Factors extending it: sector standards, high switching costs for customers, proprietary ecosystems. Note: market life may be shorter than the patent's remaining term.

t: Are there competitive or substitute products active in the market?
opts: High degree of development of competitive or substitute technologies under way
Competitive or substitute technologies are likely to be developed
50% probability that competitive technologies will be developed
Good probability of maintaining exclusivity in the market
h: Competitive analysis: monitor competitors' patents on Espacenet and Google Patents to anticipate new entrants. Barriers to entry: high R&D investment, tacit knowledge, economies of scale, network effects make substitution more difficult. High-substitution sectors: mobile apps, SaaS solutions, commoditised electronics. Low-substitution sectors: specialised industrial machinery, complex chemical processes, certified medical devices.

t: What final price is the consumer willing to pay compared to already known products?
opts: Achievable price significantly lower than competitors
h: Pricing power: a patent enabling premium pricing is the most direct sign of economic value. How to estimate: market research, conjoint analysis, A/B testing with customer samples, comparison with substitute products. Example: a patented medical device with superior clinical efficacy can justify a 30–100% premium over the generic alternative.

t: What is the potential increase in turnover in the business area thanks to the patented technology?
opts: Very small increase: 0.5% of business area turnover [value: 0.005]
h: This value enters directly into the NPV calculation as the percentage increase in business area turnover attributable to the patent. How to estimate: historical analysis of similar launches in the sector, market research, commercial pilot. For SMEs: a 4–6% increase on €1M turnover generates €40K–€60K of additional annual revenue.

t: What knowledge does the company have of the application potential and commercial opportunities?
opts: Limited knowledge only of the primary application
Poor knowledge of application and commercial potential
Good knowledge of application potential, poor commercial knowledge
Good knowledge of both application potential and commercial opportunities
Complete knowledge of all applications and commercial opportunities, including non-traditional ones
h: How to improve this score: cross-industry sector analysis, participation in technology trade fairs, scouting with EEN partners. Non-obvious applications: many technologies have uses in sectors far from the original one — this significantly expands the patent's value. Useful tool: Technology Intelligence Reports from institutes such as Fraunhofer or similar research organisations.

t: Does the patented technology have the potential to generate revenue from licence agreements?
opts: Licensing revenue possible to a limited extent
Good prospects / potential for revenue from licence agreements
Outstanding prospects: possibility of multiple licences or industry standards
h: Typical royalties by sector: pharmaceutical 5–20%, mechanical engineering 2–5%, software 5–15%, chemicals 3–8%. Licensing platforms: IAM Market, Dennemeyer Consulting, IP exchanges for finding licensees. Patent pool strategy: in sectors such as IoT, automotive, e-health, joining a patent pool can provide continuous passive income.

t: Do commercial activities require special authorisations from public bodies or similar?
opts: Authorisation needed — already refused by the public authority
Application not yet submitted or provisionally refused
Application submitted to authorities — awaiting response
Time-limited authorisation approved by the public authority
Permanent authorisation obtained, or no authorisation required to commercialise
h: Sectors with critical authorisations: pharmaceuticals (EMA/MHRA), medical devices (CE mark, class IIa–III), food (EFSA), energy, chemicals (REACH). Typical timelines: class II medical device: 12–24 months; new drug: 5–10 years; functional food: 2–4 years. Tip: start the authorisation process in parallel with technological development to reduce time-to-market.

t: Can the current output of the business area be maintained without the patented technology?
opts: 100% of output can be maintained without the patent [value: 1]
0% — the company depends entirely on the patented technology [value: 0]
h: This value enters the NPV calculation: the lower it is (more dependence), the greater the regained revenue attributable to the patent. Interpretation: if the patent protects a critical component of a core product, score 5 (total dependence) maximises the calculated NPV. Tip: be conservative in the estimate — overestimating dependence inflates NPV artificially.

t: What are the future development costs needed before commercialisation?
opts: Extremely high investment: 30% of business area turnover [0.3]
h: This value enters the NPV calculation as the annual development cost before commercialisation. What to include: residual R&D costs, patenting costs (filing, examination, validation), certification and market entry costs. Available incentives: R&D tax credits, IP Box / Patent Box regimes (UK: 10% rate; many EU countries offer similar schemes), Horizon Europe grants.

t: What is the production cost index when implementing the patented technology?
opts: 30% increase in production costs compared to current level [1.3]
No change compared to current costs [1.0]
h: This value enters directly into the NPV calculation as a multiplier of operating costs. How to estimate: compare unit production costs with and without the new technology (Activity Based Costing). Sources of cost reduction: automation, less waste, reduced cycle times, lower energy consumption. Benchmark: Industry 4.0 can lead to 10–25% cost reductions in manufacturing.

t: What investment is required for production equipment compared to the current level?
opts: 120% of current investment intensity — requires significant additional investment [1.2]
h: This value enters the NPV calculation as the production equipment investment intensity factor. How to estimate: compare the value of equipment needed with the current asset base. Leasing and rental: to reduce initial outlay, consider operating leases or long-term rental. Available funds: EIB-backed loans through partner banks, regional development funds.

t: Does the company have the financial capacity to cover renewal fees in the relevant markets?
opts: More than 15 countries / all current and potentially relevant countries
h: Indicative renewal costs (EPO, per country): years 3–5: €500–€800/year; years 6–10: €1,000–€1,500/year; years 11–15: €1,500–€2,500/year. Rationalisation strategy: every 2–3 years, check whether covered markets still generate commercial value and consider abandoning unprofitable ones. Renewal services: Dennemeyer Renewals, CPA Global, Anaqua offer automated renewal management with cost optimisation.

t: What is the estimated contribution of the patented technology to company profits?
h: How to estimate: analyse the margins of the product/service using the patent compared to the company average. IP Box regimes: income derived directly from patents, know-how and registered designs benefits from preferential tax treatment in many OECD countries (e.g. UK Patent Box at 10%; Netherlands, Luxembourg, Belgium and others offer similar schemes). IP valuation for accounts: patents with a high contribution can be recognised as assets on the balance sheet, improving financial ratios for credit access.

t: Is the patent's objective to consolidate positions in existing markets?
h: Defensive strategy: patents as entry barriers protect earned market share. Patent clustering: a portfolio of related patents ("cluster" or "thicket") makes it much harder for competitors to work around IP protection. Signal to customers: the ability to legally defend the technology increases customer confidence in supply continuity.

t: Is the patent's objective to enter new markets?
h: Patent as an internationalisation lever: a patent recognised in new geographical or application markets lowers the perceived risk for potential local partners. PCT strategy: PCT filing guarantees 30 months to decide in which countries to proceed, allowing market opportunities to be assessed before incurring nationalisation costs. EIC / EEN: support tech-based export and internationalisation through vouchers and concessional financing.

t: Is the patent part of a company image-building process?
h: The patent as a communication asset: "company with X patents" communicates innovativeness, technological strength and capacity to invest in R&D. Use in B2B marketing: certifications, innovation awards, mentions in tender specifications. Effect on bank credit: a documented IP portfolio improves creditworthiness and can unlock preferential financing.

t: Is the objective to ensure freedom to operate for future development activities?
h: Freedom to Operate (FTO): ensuring that future R&D activities do not infringe third-party patents — a defensive patent "occupies the space" before competitors do. Defensive patents: some companies file patents not to commercialise them but to prevent competitors from blocking them. Defensive publication: alternative to patenting — publishing the invention (prior art disclosure) to prevent others from patenting it, without incurring patenting costs.

t: Is the patent's objective to limit the competitive development of competitors?
h: Offensive strategy: filing patents on variants and improvements to "surround" competitors' core inventions. Caution on abuse: using the patent as an anti-competitive tool may violate EU competition law (Articles 101–102 TFEU). Standard Setting Organisations (SSOs): in standardised sectors, standard-essential patents (SEPs) must be licensed on FRAND terms.

t: Does the company use the patent for licensing or sale agreements?
h: Monetisation strategies: (1) exclusive or non-exclusive licence, (2) patent assignment (sale), (3) cross-licensing, (4) patent pooling. Patent valuation for licensing: cost, income and market approaches — a qualified IP valuator can produce a formal opinion (€3,000–€15,000). Taxation: capital gains from patent assignments may benefit from preferential treatment in many jurisdictions when reinvested in R&D.

t: Is the patent part of the company's core technology areas?
h: Core technology areas: the fundamental technologies that differentiate the company from competitors and underpin the value proposition. Balanced IP portfolio: core patents + improvement patents + defensive patents + registered designs + trade marks + know-how. IP Audit: a periodic IP portfolio audit (every 2–3 years) helps identify patents to maintain, sell or abandon — optimising maintenance costs.

t: Is there alignment between the patent and the overall company strategy?
h: Integrated IP Strategy: the patent should support the 3–5 year business objectives: geographical expansion, new markets, market share defence, licensing revenue. Periodic review: align the IP portfolio with the company strategy at each business planning cycle. Specialist support: Dennemeyer Consulting and other IP strategy advisors offer IP-business alignment workshops for SMEs.
